d.title: Not degraded — absent
d.caption: 6.3 covered parsing as a quality problem: a table flattened into orphaned numbers. This is the case where **there is no text layer to parse badly in the first place** — a chart in a paper, a diagram in a manual, a scanned filing. Standard text RAG does not get worse on these; the content simply never enters the index, so the retriever cannot return it at any k and the evaluation in §05 shows exactly that: **Hit@5 of 0.00** on image queries.

nodes.label: A chart, a diagram, a scan
Absent, not degraded
nodes.sub: which is why tuning cannot help

d.title: Summarise then embed is the structurally correct choice, not just the pragmatic one
d.caption: Option B sends each image or table to a vision model, gets a text description, and embeds **that** with the same text model as everything else. It is usually presented as a pragmatic compromise, and it is better than that: once every stored vector comes from one model, **every comparison is text-to-text in one space** — so there is no modality gap to calibrate, no cross-modal score to reconcile, and the fusion problems of 6.7 do not arise. The cost is a vision call per asset at index time, paid once.

nodes.label: Cost: one vision call per asset

d.title: ColPali removes four pipeline stages by removing extraction
d.caption: The opposite line: stop extracting anything. Treat each page as an image, embed it into **many** vectors rather than one, and compute late interaction between query tokens and page patches at query time — MaxSim, the ColBERT mechanism. What it buys is the disappearance of the four stages that caused most of this module's problems. **Chunking — 5.4's highest-leverage and fiddliest decision — does not exist**, and layout becomes a feature rather than a casualty.

items.label: No OCR
items.sub: nothing to get wrong on a scan, and no noise embedded as nonsense

items.label: No chunking
items.sub: 5.4's highest-leverage decision simply does not exist

items.label: No parsing
items.sub: no table extraction, no boilerplate stripping, no running-header bug

items.label: Layout is a feature
items.sub: a table is seen as a table; a figure sits beside its caption

d.title: Why an aggregate score is actively misleading here
d.caption: Measure each modality independently, because the aggregate hides a total failure. **Images are retrieved 0.00 of the time** and the overall Hit@5 is still a respectable-looking 0.76 — because most queries are text queries, and text works. A dashboard reporting the overall number would show a healthy system with an entire modality missing from the index, and nothing in the trend would ever reveal it.

d.title: Five ways code is not prose
d.caption: Each row breaks an assumption from module 5. **A function boundary is not a hint — it is the unit of meaning**, unlike a paragraph break, so recursive splitting on characters is simply wrong here. Understanding a function needs its imports and sometimes its callers, which is 6.4's multi-hop argument in a domain where the edges are in the syntax. And the last row breaks 6.2's nightly rebuild: a repository changes **every commit**.

items.label: Structure is strict
items.sub: a function boundary is the unit, not a hint

items.label: Dependencies cross files
items.sub: 6.4's multi-hop case, with edges in the syntax

items.label: Several representations
items.sub: raw text, AST, docstring or summary - you choose what to embed

items.label: Context is long-range
items.sub: a fix may span ten files; no top-5 covers that

items.label: It changes constantly
items.sub: every commit, not nightly - 6.2's default stops working

d.title: The relations are free, and most of them point outside the graph
d.caption: Code is the one domain where 6.4's graph needs **no extraction model at all** — calls, inherits and imports are in the syntax, so a parser recovers them exactly and the entity-resolution problem disappears. What replaces it is visible in the third row: of 372 edges, **only 116 resolve to a node inside the graph — 31%**. The rest point at the standard library, third-party packages and dynamic calls, so graph expansion mostly walks off the edge of what you indexed.

d.title: Five code embedding models, and the dimension cost nobody prices
d.caption: The first row is a good all-rounder and **3,072 dimensions is 8× the storage of 384** — 6.2's memory arithmetic applies directly, so at a million chunks that is the difference between 1.5 GB and 12 GB of RAM. The last row's 8K context is the one specification that matters structurally rather than marginally: a whole-class chunk does not fit in 512 tokens, and 5.3 measured what silent truncation does.

d.title: A stale code index is worse than a stale prose index
d.caption: 6.2 made incremental indexing by content hash the sensible default. For code it is **the only workable design**, because the slow clock is not nightly — it is every commit. And the failure is nastier than in prose: a stale code index tells you about **a function signature that no longer exists**, and the answer looks exactly as authoritative as a correct one, with a file path and a line number attached.

nodes.label: A stale entry names a dead signature
Index on the commit hook
nodes.sub: or accept answers about dead code

d.title: Six stages, and the one that is 75% of the request
d.caption: "Scale the bottleneck" is right, and 6.2 already measured where it is — which turns the list from advice into a priority order. **Re-ranking is 2,405 ms for 20 candidates on CPU: three quarters of the request.** Vector search is 11 ms, so scaling it is a *memory* decision rather than a latency one, and embedding the query is about 1% and almost never worth touching. The cheapest request remains one that never runs.

cells.text: first - the cheapest request never runs
yes - and streaming changes perception most
yes - it makes a spike degrade, not collapse

d.title: A context budget is enforceable by arithmetic, unlike most cost levers
d.caption: Generation dominates cost and generation cost scales with the retrieved context, so **the context budget is the main lever** — and unlike routing or model choice it is enforced by counting rather than estimated. At a median chunk of 99 tokens, a 3,000-token budget holds about 30 chunks and fills to **99%**; an 8,000-token budget runs out of *chunks* before it runs out of budget, filling only 51%. Which is the detail worth knowing: past some point the cap stops binding and the corpus does.

d.title: Fusion solved one of these five
d.caption: RRF genuinely settles incomparable scores — it uses rank position only, and deduplication falls out for free. The other four are untouched by it. **Source conflicts are the one people assume fusion handles**: two sources disagree on a fact, fusion ranks both highly, and says nothing whatever about which is true. That needs an explicit authority order, which is a product decision rather than a retrieval one.

items.label: Incomparable scores
items.sub: solved - RRF uses rank only, and dedupes for free

items.label: Source conflicts
items.sub: untouched - fusion ranks both and says nothing about truth

items.label: Redundant retrieval
items.sub: partly - dedupe handles copies; agentic loops need a cap

items.label: Context contention
items.sub: untouched - dedupe, re-rank and compress; do not append

items.label: Routing
items.sub: untouched - and a misroute poisons the context

d.title: Guardrails are what make the RAG promise a guarantee rather than a tendency
d.caption: The promise is precise: the answer is **grounded in retrieved context, safe, and drawn only from sources the user may see.** Each clause needs its own mechanism, and the order matters — the access check has to happen *before* retrieval, because 6.8 measures post-filtering returning 19 foreign rows, having already read them. Grounding is checked after generation, against the context that was actually supplied.

d.title: The four-part shape, and why the order is the point
d.caption: An answer that jumps to the permanent fix skips the part being tested: **whether you can stop the bleeding before you understand the cause.** Each incident in this lesson is reproduced on the corpus used throughout modules 5 and 6 — 1,187 chunks, 20 golden queries, 95% recall@5 at baseline — so every failure arrives with a measured signature rather than a description.

items.label: Symptom
items.desc: what the user or the dashboard actually reports

items.label: Immediate
items.desc: stop the bleeding, before the cause is understood

items.label: Root cause
items.desc: the measured signature, not the plausible story

items.label: Permanent
items.desc: and the check that would have caught it

d.title: Stale answers, and the 1.3 ms check that prevents them
d.caption: The symptom is a policy or price that changed yesterday and an answer still giving the old value. The cause is that the index is behind the source of truth — re-indexing is batch or manual, or the document was edited and never re-embedded. The arithmetic makes the fix obvious: **hashing twelve documents takes 1.3 ms**, re-embedding the one that changed takes 1.3 s, and rebuilding everything takes 13.2 s. The check costs a thousandth of the action it saves.

d.title: The one incident in this lesson that actually errors
d.caption: Latency spikes and OOM are the odd case: **the process dies**, so unlike every other failure here it is not silent. The causes are the index growing past memory — HNSW graphs are RAM-hungry — or `ef_search`/`nprobe` tuned up for accuracy at the cost of memory and time. The immediate move trades recall for survival; the permanent one is a **memory projection at target corpus size**, which is the check nobody runs because latency looks fine right up to the moment it does not exist.

nodes.label: Permanent: project memory at target size

d.title: Matching dimensions, mismatched models, and nothing errors
d.caption: Both models output 384 dimensions, so **the call succeeds and returns results** — ranked, scored and plausible. Recall halves from 95% to 50%, and the only signal is in the scores: mean top-1 similarity falls from **0.5698 to 0.2356**. That is why the permanent fix is a score-distribution monitor rather than a dimension check: a dimension mismatch raises, and this does not.

d.title: Identical recall, 19 leaked rows
d.caption: The two approaches score **the same on retrieval quality** — 95% recall@5 either way — and differ entirely in whether they read data the user may not see. Post-filtering searches everything and drops afterwards: 19 foreign rows entered the top 5 and were discarded *after being read*. Pre-filtering restricts the search space first and leaks nothing, **by construction rather than by diligence**. Which is the whole argument: a correctness property you get from the architecture does not depend on anyone remembering it.
